items.title: Durkheim's 1897 finding
items.claim: In Le Suicide (1897), Emile Durkheim argued that suicide rates depend on social, not individual, factors. Which pattern did he report?

options.text: Catholics had higher rates than Protestants
Protestants had higher rates than Catholics, and the unmarried higher than the married
No religious or marital differences existed
Rates were identical across all European countries

items.reveal_title: Group integration mattered more than personal pathology
items.reveal:
Durkheim correlated rates with degree of social integration. Higher integration (Catholic, married, wartime) tended to predict lower rates.

Later critics (Douglas, 1967) questioned the reliability of historical suicide records.
items.why: Durkheim's argument founded sociology as a discipline studying 'social facts' independent of individual minds.

items.title: What Marx predicted
items.claim: Karl Marx predicted that capitalism would generate growing inequality and eventual crisis. Recent empirical work (Piketty, 2014) examined wealth concentration over centuries. What was a headline finding?

options.text: Wealth inequality has steadily fallen since 1800
When the rate of return on capital exceeds growth, wealth concentrates
Inequality is impossible to measure historically

items.reveal_title: r greater than g concentrates wealth
items.reveal:
Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) used tax records across France, UK, US and others to argue that when the return on capital (r) exceeds the economic growth rate (g), inherited wealth grows faster than earned income.

The book's data and conclusions remain contested but reopened debates Marx began.
items.why: Empirical historical economics revived classical sociological questions about class structure.

items.title: Becker's central claim
items.claim: Howard Becker's Outsiders (1963) argued that deviance is not a quality of the act but of the social response. Which statement summarises his view?

options.text: Deviance is created by groups that make rules and apply them to others
Deviance is identical across all societies

items.reveal_title: The labelled act is created by the labellers
items.reveal:
Becker wrote that 'social groups create deviance by making the rules whose infraction constitutes deviance'.

His fieldwork with jazz musicians and marijuana users in 1950s Chicago shaped symbolic interactionism in criminology.
items.why: Labelling theory shifted sociological focus from offenders to the institutions that define offence.

items.title: Merton's strain typology
items.claim: Robert Merton (1938) argued that crime arises when cultural goals exceed legitimate means. How many adaptations did he identify?
items.reveal:
Merton's 1938 essay 'Social Structure and Anomie' set out five responses to the gap between goals and means.

The theory has been extended by Agnew (1992) into General Strain Theory.
items.why: Strain theory still underpins much policy thinking about inequality and crime.

items.title: Bourdieu's forms of capital
items.claim: Pierre Bourdieu argued that economic, cultural and social capital interact to reproduce class. What did he mean by 'cultural capital'?

options.text: Embodied dispositions, qualifications, and familiarity with high-status culture

items.reveal_title: Knowledge, manners and credentials function as inheritable assets
items.reveal:
Bourdieu (1986) distinguished embodied (dispositions), objectified (cultural goods) and institutionalised (qualifications) forms.

Empirical work continues to show cultural-capital indicators predict educational outcomes net of income.
items.why: Cultural capital explains why income alone underestimates the inheritance of advantage.

items.title: Willis's 'lads'
items.claim: Paul Willis's Learning to Labour (1977) studied working-class boys in a Midlands school. What did he argue they were doing through their counter-school culture?

options.text: Actively rejecting school in ways that prepared them for manual labour

items.reveal_title: Resistance that reproduced the very inequality it opposed
items.reveal:
Willis combined Marxist theory with ethnography to argue the 'lads' partially saw through school ideology but their rejection led them into the same factory jobs their fathers held.

The study influenced both education research and cultural studies.
items.why: Ethnographic fieldwork can reveal mechanisms of class reproduction invisible in statistics.

items.title: The Chicago School's method
items.claim: Robert Park and the Chicago School in the 1920s pioneered which approach to studying social life?

options.text: Urban ethnography, mapping the city as a social laboratory

items.reveal_title: The city itself as a research site
items.reveal:
Park urged students to study the 'gold coast and the slum' through direct observation. The result included Wirth's Ghetto (1928), Anderson's The Hobo (1923) and Whyte's Street Corner Society (1943).

The school established urban sociology as a recognised field.
items.why: Method choice shapes what counts as evidence and what kind of theory is possible.

items.title: UK household structure today
items.claim: What proportion of UK households in 2022 were single-person households according to the Office for National Statistics?
items.reveal_title: Roughly three in ten UK households are one person
items.reveal:
ONS data for 2022 reported around 30% of households contained a single person. The figure has risen steadily since the 1960s.

The 'standard' nuclear family is now a minority household type.
items.why: Demographic change reshapes assumptions built into policy and earlier sociological theory.

items.title: Oakley's domestic labour finding
items.claim: Ann Oakley's The Sociology of Housework (1974) interviewed 40 London housewives. What did most report about housework?

options.text: It was monotonous, low-status and isolating
It was equally shared with husbands
It was paid at market rates

items.reveal:
Oakley reported 70% of respondents expressed dissatisfaction. Her work established housework as a legitimate object of sociological study.

Later 'second shift' research (Hochschild, 1989) extended the analysis to employed women.
items.why: Recognising unpaid labour as work reframed measurements of economic activity.

items.title: Goffman's dramaturgy
items.claim: Erving Goffman's The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959) used what extended metaphor to analyse social interaction?

options.text: Theatrical performance with front-stage and back-stage

items.reveal_title: Life as performance with managed appearances
items.reveal:
Goffman drew on theatre to describe 'front' (managed self) and 'back' (off-stage) regions. His later work on stigma (1963) and institutions (1961) extended the framework.

The approach is now standard in microsociology.
items.why: Theatrical metaphors gave sociology vocabulary for the moment-to-moment work of social life.

items.title: Weber's iron cage
items.claim: Max Weber argued modernity was driven by rationalisation. What did his 'iron cage' (stahlhartes Gehause) refer to?

options.text: The bureaucratic and economic systems constraining individual freedom in modern society

items.reveal_title: Bureaucratic rationality as a constraining structure
items.reveal:
In The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), Weber argued the rational pursuit of efficiency would outlast the religious motives that birthed it, trapping moderns in a structure they could not easily escape.

Parsons's English translation 'iron cage' is now standard; 'shell as hard as steel' is closer to the German.
items.why: Translation shapes how foundational concepts travel between languages and disciplines.

items.title: Foucault's panopticon
items.claim: Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (1975) used what 18th-century architectural design to illustrate modern power?
items.reveal_title: Bentham's never-built prison became a model of modern surveillance
items.reveal:
Bentham proposed the panopticon in 1791 as a circular building where inmates could be observed at any moment without knowing when.

Foucault argued the principle, the internalisation of an unseen watcher, had spread to schools, factories and clinics.
items.why: Power in modernity, Foucault argued, often works through visibility rather than coercion.

items.title: Moral panics
items.claim: Stanley Cohen's Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972) studied which group?

options.text: Mods and rockers at English seaside resorts in 1964

items.reveal_title: Bank holiday disturbances at Clacton and Brighton
items.reveal:
Cohen analysed how relatively minor incidents in 1964 were amplified by press coverage, generating reactions out of proportion to the original events.

The model has since been applied to repeated panics around drugs, immigration and youth culture.
items.why: Cohen's framework still organises how sociologists study media-driven public reactions.

items.title: Disadvantage gap in England
items.claim: England's 'disadvantage gap' tracks attainment of pupils eligible for free school meals against peers. After narrowing in the 2010s, what happened from 2019?

options.text: It widened, including after pandemic disruption
It reversed: FSM pupils overtook peers

items.reveal:
Education Policy Institute analyses reported the disadvantage gap at GCSE widened from 2019, reaching its widest in over a decade by 2022.

Pandemic-related school closures appear to have amplified pre-existing trends.
items.why: Apparent progress can reverse when systems are stressed, revealing structural fragility.
